subsection: 5. Moves towards European unity and the EEC, 1945–1992

notes.h: Why Western Europeans wanted unity after 1945
notes.b: In 1945 Western Europe was in ruins and its old rivalries had just caused a second world war. Leaders turned to unity for three reasons: to stop another war, to stand together against the Soviet Union and to rebuild their economies.
points: The Second World War left Western Europe devastated and dependent on the USA. France and Germany had fought three wars in seventy years (1870-71, 1914 and 1939), so ending their rivalry was the first aim of unity.

The Cold War split Europe by the Iron Curtain into a Soviet bloc in the East and a Western side, which formed NATO (the US-led military alliance) in April 1949. Integration here was Western European only, and its supporters saw it as strength against the Soviet threat.

Marshall Aid (1948-52) and the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC, set up in 1948 to share it out) made the USA a sponsor of European cooperation, because Americans wanted the Europeans to plan their recovery together.

Economic recovery was a third motive: a larger market allows more efficient production, and the Benelux customs union (Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg, in force 1 January 1948) was an example that cooperation worked.

The Federal Republic of Germany (West Germany) was founded in 1949 under its first chancellor, Konrad Adenauer (in office 1949-63). How to rebuild and rearm it safely, the 'German question', lay behind both the Schuman Plan and the European Defence Community.
Ideas mattered too. Altiero Spinelli, an Italian federalist, wrote the Ventotene Manifesto in 1941 while interned by Mussolini's regime.

Christian Democrat leaders such as Robert Schuman (France), Adenauer and Alcide De Gasperi (Italy) shared a wish to bind their countries together, and Europe's decline as a world power made unity look necessary.
notes.tip: When asked why the EEC was established, link the causes to what followed: peace between France and Germany, the Soviet threat, recovery, American encouragement and federalist ideas, then the chain of ECSC, failed EDC, Messina and Rome.

notes.h: The vocabulary of unity: common market, federal Europe and the rest
notes.b: The history of European unity is a debate between two ways of organising it, and a handful of terms describe the choices. Knowing them lets you say exactly what each treaty did and what each leader wanted.
points: A federal Europe means a united Europe with a central, supranational government above the national governments. Federalists such as Spinelli, Spaak, Monnet, Hallstein and Delors wanted this.
Supranational means that the institutions' decisions bind member states, even against their wishes. Examples are the ECSC High Authority, the Commission and the Court of Justice.

Intergovernmental means cooperation decided by national governments, each keeping a veto (the power to block a decision). The Council of Europe, EFTA, de Gaulle's Europe of states and Thatcher's view all follow this model.

A customs union has no tariffs (taxes on imports) between members and one common tariff on goods from outside. It is the first stage of a common market, which adds free movement of goods, services, capital and people. In Britain and Ireland the EEC was commonly called 'the Common Market'.

The single market is the completion of the common market by removing physical (border), technical (standards) and fiscal (tax) barriers, the 1992 programme. Do not confuse it with the customs union, completed in 1968.
Qualified majority voting means decisions in the Council of Ministers by a weighted majority rather than unanimity, so one state cannot block everything. The Single European Act extended it.
The Six were France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg, the members of the ECSC and the founders of the EEC.
notes.tip: Examiners reward answers that sort developments into supranational (coal and steel, trade) and intergovernmental (most other things), so use these two words in any 'how far' question.

notes.h: Early cooperation and the Council of Europe, 1946-1953
notes.b: Between 1946 and 1950 Europeans tried loose cooperation first. It produced a forum for debate, not a government, and its limits pushed the federalists to look for another route.
points: Winston Churchill, then leader of the opposition, called at the University of Zurich on 19 September 1946 for 'a kind of United States of Europe' built on a partnership between France and Germany. He saw Britain and the Commonwealth as friends and sponsors outside it, not members.
The Congress of Europe at The Hague (May 1948) brought together several hundred delegates, with Churchill as chairman. It called for a European assembly and a charter of human rights.
It split between federalists, who wanted real authority, and unionists, who wanted cooperation between governments, so it showed the argument that ran through the whole period.

The Council of Europe was founded by the Treaty of London on 5 May 1949 by ten states: Belgium, Denmark, France, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and Britain. Its seat is Strasbourg.

Its Consultative Assembly could only debate and recommend, so it was a forum rather than a source of binding law. This disappointed federalists, and Paul-Henri Spaak, the Assembly's first president (1949), resigned in 1951 in frustration at its lack of power.
Its main achievement was the European Convention on Human Rights, signed in Rome on 4 November 1950 and in force in 1953. The European Court of Human Rights was set up in Strasbourg in 1959.
The Council of Europe is not an EEC institution, and its Court of Human Rights is not the EEC's Court of Justice (which sits in Luxembourg). Do not confuse either with the Council of Ministers.
notes.tip: A common slip is to treat the Council of Europe as part of the EEC. It is a separate, intergovernmental body, and examiners expect you to say why federalists found it too weak.

notes.b: Monnet was a French planner and persuader who designed the first European communities and is widely called a 'father of Europe'. He never held elected office, so he worked through politicians.
points: He was born in Cognac, France, in 1888, worked in the family cognac business and then in international finance, and was deputy secretary-general of the League of Nations from 1919 to 1923.

In the Second World War he coordinated Anglo-French war supplies (1939-40) and helped draft the offer of a Franco-British union in June 1940, which the French government did not accept before France's surrender. He later worked on war supplies in Washington.

From 1946 he headed the French planning commission. The Monnet Plan of that year modernised coal, steel, electricity, transport and other basic industries through state investment, partly financed by Marshall Aid.

He drafted the Schuman Declaration, announced by the foreign minister Robert Schuman on 9 May 1950. His method was to unite Europe sector by sector, 'through concrete achievements', so that each small step created a reason for the next.
He was the first president of the ECSC High Authority (1952-55), based in Luxembourg. He then left it to campaign for further integration.

In 1955 he founded the Action Committee for the United States of Europe, which brought together political parties and trade unions from the Six. It pressed for Euratom, the EEC and later British membership, so he kept shaping events without office.
Contemporaries were divided. Federalists and American leaders admired him, while de Gaulle and the Gaullists opposed him because they rejected supranational institutions. He died in 1979.
Historians call him the architect of the 'Monnet method' of gradual, functional integration, but debate how much credit he deserves compared with the national governments that took the decisions.
notes.tip: For a short answer give his career in order with one fact per point: League 1919-23, Plan 1946, Declaration 1950, High Authority 1952-55, Action Committee 1955. End with his significance. Remember he drafted the Declaration but Schuman announced it.

notes.h: The Schuman Plan and the European Coal and Steel Community
notes.b: The first supranational community pooled the coal and steel of France and West Germany. It was designed so that the two old enemies could not make war on each other without the other noticing.
points: Coal and steel were the basis of war industries, and they were a sore point: the Ruhr (in West Germany) had been under an International Authority for the Ruhr since 1949, and the Saar was under French economic control after the war (it returned to West Germany in 1957).

The Schuman Declaration of 9 May 1950 proposed a joint authority for French and West German coal and steel, open to other states. It said pooling them would make war between France and Germany 'not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible'. 9 May is now celebrated as Europe Day.

Reactions differed. Adenauer accepted at once, because the plan treated West Germany as an equal and offered an end to international control of the Ruhr (that authority was wound up only when the ECSC began in 1952). Italy and the Benelux countries joined.
Britain's Labour government under Clement Attlee refused to join, because it would not hand control of its nationalised coal and steel industries to a supranational body.
The Treaty of Paris was signed on 18 April 1951 by the Six (the signatories) and came into force on 23 July 1952, to run for fifty years.
It had four institutions: the High Authority (a supranational executive), the Common Assembly, the Special Council of Ministers and the Court of Justice.

The High Authority could take decisions binding on firms and governments, raise a levy on coal and steel production and fine firms that broke the rules. Because it did not need each government's consent for these, it was truly supranational.

Results: a common market in coal and steel, an institutional model that the EEC later copied, and Franco-German reconciliation in practice, since the two countries now ran their war industries together.
notes.tip: Keep the dates apart: Schuman Declaration (May 1950), Treaty of Paris (April 1951), ECSC in operation (1952). Also remember that Monnet drafted and Schuman announced.

notes.h: The failure of the European Defence Community
notes.b: After success in coal and steel, the French tried to extend the same supranational method to defence. The attempt failed, and integration turned back to the economy.
points: The Korean War (from June 1950) led the USA to press for West German rearmament. In October 1950 the French prime minister René Pleven proposed a European Defence Community (EDC), a European army, so that West Germany could rearm without having a national army.
The EDC Treaty was signed on 27 May 1952 by the Six. A plan for a European Political Community (1953) depended on it and fell with it.
The French National Assembly rejected the EDC on 30 August 1954, by a procedural vote. It was the Assembly, not the government, that killed a plan the French government itself had proposed.

The reasons were fear of German rearmament, opposition from Gaullists and communists, and reluctance to lose sovereignty over the army. Britain had refused to join, and the death of Stalin in March 1953 and the Korean armistice of July 1953 had eased the sense of threat.

West Germany was rearmed another way. The Paris Agreements of October 1954 extended the 1948 Brussels Treaty to West Germany and Italy, creating the Western European Union (from 1955), and West Germany joined NATO in May 1955.
The result was that integration turned back to economics, and defence stayed national and Atlantic. This is why the Treaties of Rome were about trade, not armies.
notes.tip: Learn the three stages as separate dates: the Pleven Plan (1950), the EDC Treaty (1952) and the French rejection (1954). Say it was the National Assembly that rejected it, not the government.

notes.h: Messina, the Treaties of Rome and the EEC
notes.b: Having failed in defence, the Six returned to the economy in 1955. The result, the Treaties of Rome, created the EEC, which became the centre of European integration.
points: The Messina conference of the six foreign ministers (1-3 June 1955) relaunched the project. It was prepared by the Benelux governments and chaired by Italy; Monnet was not its organiser but worked through his Action Committee.
Spaak chaired the committee whose report (April 1956) proposed a common market and an atomic energy community. It was approved at Venice in May 1956.

The Treaties of Rome were signed on 25 March 1957 by the Six and came into force on 1 January 1958. They created the European Economic Community (EEC) and the European Atomic Energy Community (Euratom).

The EEC was to build a customs union in stages over twelve years, with a common external tariff, and to bring free movement of goods, services, capital and workers (the 'four freedoms'). It also planned common policies in agriculture and transport.
The preamble speaks of 'an ever closer union among the peoples of Europe', which shows that the long-term aim was political as well as economic.
Euratom was for civil nuclear cooperation among the Six. It was less important than the EEC.

Four institutions ran the EEC: the Commission (based in Brussels, which proposed legislation), the Council of Ministers, the Assembly and the Court of Justice. The Assembly renamed itself the European Parliament in 1962, and its members were appointed from national parliaments until direct elections in 1979.

Walter Hallstein of West Germany, a federalist, was the first Commission president (1958-67). The Merger Treaty (signed 1965, in force 1 July 1967) merged the executives of the ECSC, EEC and Euratom into one Commission and one Council.
The EEC was not the European Union or a single currency. Those date from Maastricht (1992, in force 1993) and the euro from 1999.
notes.tip: Keep the treaties apart: Treaty of London (1949, Council of Europe), Treaty of Paris (1951, ECSC), Paris Agreements (1954, WEU) and Treaties of Rome (1957, EEC and Euratom). Ordinary Level questions often ask just for the treaty that created the EEC and its year.

notes.h: Building the EEC: the CAP, the customs union and EFTA
notes.b: In its first decade the EEC proved it could deliver. It built its customs union early and launched a common farm policy, while a rival group tried a looser path.
points: The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) was agreed in January 1962 and operated from 1962, designed by the Dutch commissioner Sicco Mansholt. It gave farmers common guaranteed prices, protected them with a levy on cheaper imports and paid export subsidies, all financed from a common fund.

Benefits were secure incomes for farmers and food security. Costs were that the CAP became by far the largest item in the Community budget, and guaranteed prices produced surpluses nicknamed 'butter mountains' and 'wine lakes'. Milk quotas were introduced in 1984 to limit them.
The customs union was completed on 1 July 1968, eighteen months ahead of schedule, with the common external tariff in place the same day. Trade among the Six grew rapidly.

The European Free Trade Association (EFTA) was set up by the Stockholm Convention in January 1960 (in force May 1960) by Britain, Austria, Denmark, Norway, Portugal, Sweden and Switzerland. It was a free-trade area in industrial goods only, with no common external tariff and no supranational institutions.

EFTA was Britain's alternative to the EEC for states that rejected supranationalism. Its weakness was that it lacked the EEC's large common market and common policies, so Britain, Ireland and Denmark applied to join the EEC in 1961.
notes.tip: For effects of unity, separate economic effects (trade, markets, farming under the CAP, regional funds) from political and social ones, and balance the CAP's benefits for farmers against its cost and surpluses. Do not give percentages for the CAP's budget share.

notes.h: De Gaulle, the vetoes and the empty chair crisis
notes.b: Charles de Gaulle, president of France from 1959 to 1969, wanted a Europe of cooperating states, not a supranational one. He used vetoes and a boycott to block British entry and to defend national sovereignty.
points: De Gaulle favoured a Europe of states or nations, cooperation between sovereign governments, which contrasted with Monnet's supranational model. He is often said to have used the phrase 'Europe des patries', but he denied it.
The Élysée Treaty of Franco-German friendship, signed on 22 January 1963 by de Gaulle and Adenauer, showed that he wanted a French-led partnership with West Germany at the heart of Europe.

Britain applied to join in 1961 under Harold Macmillan (the negotiator was Edward Heath), as did Ireland under Seán Lemass and Denmark. De Gaulle announced his veto at a press conference on 14 January 1963.

His reasons were Britain's ties to the USA (the Nassau agreement of December 1962 on American Polaris missiles for Britain) and to the Commonwealth, and its different farming and trading system. He feared Britain would weaken the Community and French leadership of it.
He vetoed Britain, not Ireland. Ireland's application lapsed because its trade depended on the British market, so it would not join without Britain.
Britain reapplied in 1967 under Harold Wilson, with Ireland and Denmark, and de Gaulle used his second veto on 27 November 1967.

The empty chair crisis began when France stopped attending Council of Ministers meetings from 30 June / 1 July 1965. The causes were the financing of the CAP, plans to give the Commission and Assembly control of Community money, and the coming move to majority voting.

The Luxembourg Compromise of January 1966 was an informal political agreement, not a treaty change. Where a member said very important national interests were at stake, the Council would try for unanimity. In practice a state could block such decisions, so unanimity became the norm for about twenty years.
notes.tip: Keep the two vetoes apart (14 January 1963 against Macmillan's application, 27 November 1967 against Wilson's) and the empty chair (1965) apart from the Luxembourg Compromise (1966). Do not say the Compromise gave a legal veto.

notes.b: After de Gaulle resigned in April 1969, his successor Georges Pompidou allowed the Community to grow. The 1970s brought new members and new institutions, but also slow progress.
points: The Hague summit of 1-2 December 1969 agreed on 'completion, deepening, enlargement': finishing the common policies, moving towards monetary union and admitting new members. Do not confuse it with the Hague Congress of 1948.
Britain (prime minister Edward Heath), Ireland (Taoiseach Jack Lynch) and Denmark joined on 1 January 1973. Norway's voters rejected membership in September 1972.

Irish voters approved membership in a referendum on 10 May 1972 by about 83 per cent. Britain confirmed its membership in a referendum on 5 June 1975 under Harold Wilson, when about two-thirds voted to stay in. Britain joined in 1973, not 1975.

The European Regional Development Fund was set up in 1975 to help poorer regions. Ireland later became a large net beneficiary of the CAP and the structural funds, so it was an informal bargain rather than a legal right.

The European Monetary System (EMS) began on 13 March 1979, with the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM), which kept currencies within bands, and the ECU, a unit of account. Roy Jenkins, Commission president 1977-81, promoted it, backed by Helmut Schmidt and Valery Giscard d'Estaing.
Ireland joined the ERM, and the Irish pound's one-to-one link with sterling ended in March 1979. Britain stayed out until October 1990 and left in September 1992.
The first direct elections to the European Parliament were held in June 1979, giving it a democratic mandate for the first time.
Eurosclerosis was the name for the slow progress of the Community in the 1970s and early 1980s, during recession.
notes.tip: Show change as uneven. The 1970s mix enlargement, the EMS and direct elections with Eurosclerosis, and examiners rate this kind of judgement more than a list of treaties.

notes.h: The 1980s: Mediterranean enlargement, the budget and the Single European Act
notes.b: In the 1980s the Community widened to twelve members and then deepened, setting a deadline for a true single market. Britain's budget quarrel had to be settled first.
points: Greece joined on 1 January 1981, after military rule ended in 1974. Spain and Portugal joined on 1 January 1986, after the fall of dictatorship (Franco died in 1975; Portugal's dictatorship fell in 1974). Membership became twelve, and the Community supported these new democracies.

At the Fontainebleau summit in June 1984 a permanent rebate for Britain on its budget contribution was agreed, which settled a dispute that had dogged the Community. This was needed so that the Community could move on to other business.

The Single European Act was signed in February 1986 and came into force on 1 July 1987. Its entry into force was delayed by the Irish Supreme Court's Crotty judgment, which required a referendum, and the Irish referendum of May 1987 approved it.

The Act set 31 December 1992 for the single market, extended qualified majority voting, gave the Parliament more say and put European Political Cooperation (foreign policy) on a treaty basis. Structural funds doubled afterwards.
Germany reunified on 3 October 1990, and the former East Germany became part of the Community through the united Germany. This mattered because it enlarged the market.

notes.b: Delors was the French socialist who led the European Commission for ten years and relaunched integration through the single market and the plan for monetary union.
points: He was born in Paris in 1925 and worked at the Banque de France and in French planning. A socialist influenced by Catholic social thought, he joined the Socialist Party in 1974.

He advised prime minister Jacques Chaban-Delmas (1969-72), was an MEP (1979-81) and was French minister of the economy and finance under President Mitterrand (1981-84), so he came to Brussels with government experience.
He was president of the European Commission from January 1985 to January 1995, three terms, about ten years.

The single market was his first project: the 1985 White Paper listed about 300 measures to remove physical, technical and fiscal barriers by 31 December 1992, and the Single European Act of 1986 gave it legal force.

He added a social dimension, because he thought a single market needed protection for workers. In September 1988 he told the British Trades Union Congress to expect one, and the Social Charter was adopted in December 1989 by eleven of the twelve members, Britain refusing.
In July 1988 he told the European Parliament that within ten years about 80 per cent of economic legislation would come from the Community, which is why opponents feared a loss of sovereignty.
The Delors Report of April 1989 set out economic and monetary union in three stages. He took part in the Maastricht negotiations of 1991 and the Treaty of 1992, which built on his plan.

Contemporaries credited him with relaunching the Community after Eurosclerosis. Thatcher saw him as the leader of a drive towards a European super-state, and the Sun newspaper's headline 'Up Yours Delors' (1990) showed British tabloid hostility.
Historians rate him one of the most influential Commission presidents, but debate whether his federal ambitions outran what member states and voters wanted, as the Danish 'no' of 1992 suggested.
notes.tip: Give his career in order with one fact per point: finance minister 1981-84, Commission 1985-95, SEA 1986, Delors Report 1989, Maastricht 1992. Do not call him the longest-serving president, because he served ten years and three terms.

notes.b: Maastricht turned the Community into a union with the aim of a single currency. It also exposed how far voters and governments were willing to go.
points: The Treaty on European Union was agreed at Maastricht in December 1991, signed on 7 February 1992 and in force on 1 November 1993. It created the European Union, so the term dates from here, not from Rome.

The Union had three pillars: the European Communities, a Common Foreign and Security Policy, and cooperation in justice and home affairs. The principle of subsidiarity (decisions taken at the lowest suitable level) was added.
Economic and monetary union would come in three stages, with a single currency by 1 January 1999 at the latest, and the treaty introduced European citizenship.
Britain opted out of the single currency and the Social Chapter (the Maastricht protocol on social policy, not to be confused with the 1989 Social Charter declaration). Denmark later gained opt-outs.
Danish voters rejected the treaty on 2 June 1992 (approving it in a second vote in 1993), while Irish voters approved it in June 1992.
notes.tip: Single European Act (1986, in force 1987) and Maastricht (1992, in force 1993) are often confused, so give each its own date and content.

notes.h: Attitudes to unity: federalists, intergovernmentalists and Britain
notes.b: Throughout the period people disagreed about what unity should be. The split was between those who wanted a federal Europe and those who wanted cooperation between states.
points: Federalists (Spinelli, Spaak, Monnet, Hallstein and Delors) wanted supranational institutions. Intergovernmentalists (de Gaulle, Thatcher and British governments generally) wanted states to keep control. This split explains most disputes in the period.

Thatcher, British prime minister 1979-90, supported the single market and signed the Single European Act, but opposed federalism, the social dimension and a single currency. She demanded a refund of what she called Britain's own money.
In her Bruges speech of 20 September 1988 she said Europe should be a family of sovereign nations and warned against 'a European super-state' exercising power from Brussels.
Britain was called an 'awkward partner', the title of a book by the historian Stephen George (1990), because of its late entry, the referendum, the budget dispute and the opt-outs.
notes.tip: Do not say Thatcher opposed the single market. Show each person's actions as well as their views: Thatcher's rebate, Bruges speech and opt-out stance; Monnet's Plan and High Authority; Delors's SEA, Social Charter and EMU plan.

notes.b: Unity changed Western Europe's economy, politics and society, but not equally for everyone. Weigh the benefits against the costs.
points: Economic: trade between members grew rapidly, markets and investment grew, farmers got guaranteed prices under the CAP, and the regional and structural funds helped poorer regions such as Ireland. The costs were CAP surpluses and food prices.

Political: there was Franco-German reconciliation and no war between members of the Community in the period. Spain, Portugal and Greece joined as new democracies, and Europe gained a stronger voice in world trade.
Social: free movement of workers and common rules on working conditions and equal pay (women's rights belong elsewhere) gave new opportunities to countries such as Ireland.

Limits: unity was Western Europe only, there was no common defence, national vetoes remained, the CAP was costly, and there was a 'democratic deficit' (the Parliament had limited power over decisions). This is why unity did not reach every area.
notes.tip: Effects questions reward separating economic from social and political effects and balancing them with costs such as surpluses, loss of sovereignty and the democratic deficit.

notes.h: Assessment: how far did Europe move towards unity, 1945-1992?
notes.b: A good answer opens with a judgement. Economic unity went far, but political and defence unity did not, and Europe was supranational in coal, steel and trade but intergovernmental in most else.
points: Achievements: peace between France and Germany, a customs union and single market, growth from six to twelve members and democracy anchored in the south.
Limits: no common defence (the EDC failed), de Gaulle's vetoes and the empty chair, the CAP's costs, Britain's reluctance, and unity confined to Western Europe.
Contemporary view: federalists hoped that Maastricht was the start of a political union, while critics such as Thatcher feared a super-state.
Later view: historians stress that integration came from compromises between national governments, not from the triumph of the Monnet method alone.

On Monnet and Delors, contemporaries saw them as builders of peace or as threats to sovereignty, while historians ask how far they or the governments deserve the credit and whether Delors's ambitions outran voters.
notes.tip: Examiners reward paired points, achievements against limits and contemporary against later views, with a clear judgement and a view of who was most influential.

keyTerms.definition: A trading area in which goods, services, capital and workers move freely between member states, with common external tariffs.
The vision of a united Europe with supranational institutions and a central authority, opposed by intergovernmentalists who wanted national governments to decide.
The 1951 community that pooled French, West German, Italian and Benelux coal and steel production under a supranational High Authority.
The French boycott of the EEC Council of Ministers from June 1965 over the CAP and the powers of the Commission.
The January 1966 agreement that let member states use a veto on matters they regarded as vital national interests.
The 1986 treaty that set the goal of a single market by 1992 and extended majority voting in the EEC.
The 1979 arrangement that linked member currencies through fixed exchange rate bands, forerunner of the single currency.
Describing institutions, like the ECSC High Authority and the Commission, whose decisions bind member states and which stand above national governments.
The view that European cooperation should be decided by national governments, which keep their veto, rather than by central institutions.
The EEC's system, begun in 1962, of common farm prices and support for farmers, financed from a common budget.
A group of states that remove tariffs between themselves and impose a common tariff on imports from outside.

factCards.definition: On 9 May 1950 Robert Schuman proposed pooling French and West German coal and steel under a joint authority.

factCards.term: Treaty of Paris, 1951: signatories and date
factCards.definition: Signed on 18 April 1951 by France, West Germany, Italy and the Benelux countries, creating the ECSC.
The French National Assembly rejected the European Defence Community on 30 August 1954.

factCards.term: Treaties of Rome: signing and entry into force
factCards.definition: Signed on 25 March 1957 and in force from 1 January 1958, creating the EEC and Euratom.
The June 1955 conference at Messina relaunched European integration after the EDC failure.

factCards.term: De Gaulle's first veto of Britain: date
factCards.definition: De Gaulle vetoed British EEC membership on 14 January 1963.
France withdrew its representatives from the EEC Council of Ministers in June 1965.
Britain, Ireland and Denmark joined the EEC on 1 January 1973.
Spain and Portugal joined on 1 January 1986, bringing membership to twelve.
Britain's budget rebate was agreed at the Fontainebleau summit in June 1984.
Signed on 7 February 1992, it created the European Union and set a timetable for economic and monetary union.
The 1989 report set out a three-stage route to economic and monetary union.
The Monnet Plan for French modernisation (1946), the drafting of the Schuman Declaration (1950) and the presidency of the ECSC High Authority (1952–55).
The Single European Act and the 1992 single market programme, the 1989 Delors Report on monetary union, and the Social Charter of 1989.
